questions.question: Define pneumatics and hydraulics, explain what pressure is, and give two everyday examples of each system.
questions.expected_answer: Pneumatics uses a gas, usually compressed air, to transmit force and movement; hydraulics uses a liquid, usually oil or water. Pressure is force divided by the area it acts on, and in a sealed fluid system the pressure applied at one point is felt throughout the fluid. Pneumatic examples: bus doors, tyre pumps, truck air brakes, nail guns, dentists' drills. Hydraulic examples: trolley jacks, car brakes, excavator arms, dentist chairs, the Jaws of Life.

questions.question: Two syringes of different sizes are joined by a tube and filled with water. Explain why pushing the small plunger produces a larger force at the large plunger and what is lost in exchange.
questions.expected_answer: The force on the small plunger creates a pressure in the water, and because the water cannot be compressed and is sealed in, the same pressure acts on the face of the large plunger. The large face has a greater area, so the same pressure produces a greater force, in proportion to the ratio of the areas; a face four times larger gives four times the force. In exchange the large plunger moves a shorter distance, one quarter as far for four times the area, because the volume of water leaving the small syringe equals the volume entering the large one.

questions.question: Explain the difference in behaviour between air and water when compressed, and use it to justify why a rescue tool is hydraulic while a bus door is pneumatic.
questions.expected_answer: Air can be compressed because its particles are far apart; a blocked air-filled syringe pushes in and springs back. Water cannot be compressed noticeably because its particles are already in contact; a blocked water-filled syringe will not move. A rescue tool must transmit force immediately and precisely and hold a heavy load without springing, so it uses an incompressible liquid. A bus door needs only a light, quick movement, benefits from the gentle springiness of air, and air is free, light and harmless if it leaks, so it is pneumatic.
